title: Foundational Computational Tools for Bioengineers
text:
Preface
Welcome to Foundational Computational Tools for Bioengineers, a comprehensive guide designed to equip graduate students with essential computational skills for modern research in biology, bioengineering, and related life sciences.

title: Foundational Computational Tools for Bioengineers
text:
Why This Book?
Modern scientific research is fundamentally computational. Whether you’re analyzing genomic sequences, processing microscopy images, modeling biological systems, or managing experimental data, computational literacy has become as essential as laboratory technique. Yet many graduate students enter their programs without formal training in these foundational skills.
This book bridges that gap by providing a practical, hands-on introduction to the core computational tools you’ll use throughout your scientific career.






TipLearning Philosophy



This is a practical course, and we will learn by doing. Each chapter includes worked examples, exercises, and real-world applications drawn from bioengineering and life sciences research.

title: Foundational Computational Tools for Bioengineers
text:
What You Will Learn
By the end of this book, you will be able to:

Understand computer architecture and choose appropriate computing resources for your analyses
Navigate file systems and automate tasks using Unix/Linux commands
Write shell scripts to create reproducible analysis pipelines
Process and analyze large biological datasets using command-line tools
Program in R for statistical analysis and data visualization
Program in Python with NumPy, pandas, and matplotlib, and translate between R and Python idioms
Apply tidy data principles for effective data management
Use Git and GitHub for version control and collaboration
Submit and manage jobs on high-performance computing clusters

title: Foundational Computational Tools for Bioengineers
text:
Prerequisites
No prior programming experience is required! However, you should have:

Access to a computer running Windows, macOS, or Linux
Willingness to learn through practice and experimentation
Patience with yourself as you develop new skills

title: Foundational Computational Tools for Bioengineers
text:
How to Use This Book
Each chapter builds on previous material, so I recommend reading them in order, at least initially, starting with 1  Introduction to Computational Tools and the software setup in 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs. The appendices (Appendix A — Keyboard Shortcuts Reference through Appendix J — Glossary) are look-up references to return to as you work. Key features include:


Callout boxes highlighting important concepts, tips, and warnings

Code examples that you can copy and modify for your own work

Practice exercises to reinforce your learning

Cross-references connecting related concepts across chapters







TipHands-On Practice



The best way to learn computational skills is to type the commands yourself. Avoid copying and pasting when possible—the muscle memory of typing commands is part of the learning process.

title: 1  Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
1.1 The Computational Revolution in Biology
Modern biological research has undergone a profound transformation. The advent of high-throughput technologies—from next-generation sequencing to automated microscopy to mass spectrometry—has generated an explosion of data that far exceeds what can be analyzed manually. Consider these examples:
To make sense of this data deluge, researchers must be fluent in computational tools. This fluency goes beyond simply running pre-made software—it requires understanding how to manipulate data, automate analyses, and ensure reproducibility.

title: 1  Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
A single human genome sequence contains approximately 6 billion base pairs

A typical RNA-seq experiment generates tens of millions of short reads
Proteomics studies can identify and quantify thousands of proteins simultaneously
High-content imaging screens produce terabytes of image data

title: 1  Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
1.2 Why Learn Computational Skills?
There are compelling reasons to invest time in developing computational proficiency:
Speed and Scale. Computational tools allow you to perform thousands of operations with single commands. Tasks that would take days by hand can be completed in seconds.
Reproducibility. Scripts and code serve as a complete record of your analysis. Unlike clicking through graphical interfaces, command-line workflows can be exactly reproduced, shared, and verified (Sandve et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2017).
Flexibility. General-purpose programming languages can handle virtually any data format or analysis type. You’re not limited to what software developers anticipated.
Access to Specialized Tools. Many cutting-edge analysis tools in bioinformatics are only available through the command line. Learning to use the shell opens doors to thousands of free programs developed by scientists for scientists.
High-Performance Computing. Large-scale analyses require computing clusters. These systems are accessed and controlled through command-line interfaces.






TipCareer Impact



Computational skills are increasingly valued in academic and industry positions. Investing in these skills now will pay dividends throughout your career. Organizing your computational projects well from the start saves countless hours later (Noble, 2009).

title: 1  Introduction to Computational Tools
section: 1.3 Coding vs. Scripting: What’s the Difference?
text:
1.3 Coding vs. Scripting: What’s the Difference?
You’ll often hear the terms “coding” and “scripting” used interchangeably, but there are technical distinctions worth understanding.
Compiled Languages (Coding)
Compiled languages require a separate compilation step that translates human-readable source code into machine code before execution. Examples include:

C/C++
Fortran
Rust
Go

The compilation process produces optimized executable files that run very quickly. However, compiled languages typically require more setup and are less forgiving of errors during development.
Interpreted Languages (Scripting)
Interpreted languages (or scripting languages) execute code line-by-line at runtime, without a separate compilation step. Examples include:

Bash/Shell
Python
R
Julia
Perl

Interpreted languages offer greater flexibility and faster development cycles at the cost of some execution speed. They’re ideal for data analysis, automation, and interactive exploration.






Note



The distinction between compiled and interpreted languages has become increasingly blurred. Modern systems like Julia use just-in-time (JIT) compilation to achieve near-compiled performance with scripting-language convenience. Python and R can also interface with compiled C/C++ code for performance-critical operations.


Which Should You Learn?
For most biological research, interpreted languages are the right choice. They enable rapid prototyping and experimentation—you can try an idea, see if it works, and refine it immediately. Their interactive nature makes them ideal for data exploration, allowing you to probe your data and understand its structure before committing to a particular analysis approach. The scientific computing community has developed extensive libraries for these languages, from statistical methods to machine learning to bioinformatics pipelines. And because interpreted languages tend to have more forgiving syntax and immediate feedback, they present lower barriers to entry for beginners.
In this course, we work primarily with Bash (the Unix shell) and R, with Python installed and used alongside them, and with exposure to high-performance computing concepts that may eventually lead you to compiled languages if your research requires it.

title: 1  Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
1.4 Tools We Will Cover
This book and accompanying course introduce you to a carefully selected set of tools that form the foundation of computational research in the life sciences (Buffalo, 2015).
Unix/Linux and the Shell
The Unix shell (specifically Bash) provides a powerful interface for file manipulation that goes far beyond what graphical file managers offer. It includes specialized tools for processing large text-based data files—essential when working with genomic sequences, tabular data, or log files. Perhaps most importantly, the shell lets you combine simple programs into complex workflows through pipes and scripting, and it provides access to remote computing systems using the same commands you use locally. Understanding Unix is essential because it underlies most scientific computing infrastructure, from laptops to supercomputers. The shell is introduced in Chapter 4 and developed through Chapter 10.
R Statistical Programming
R is a programming language and environment specifically designed for statistical computing and graphics (R Core Team, 2024). It provides comprehensive statistical analysis capabilities, from basic descriptive statistics to advanced machine learning algorithms. R excels at producing publication-quality graphics with fine-grained control over every visual element. The community has developed thousands of packages for specialized analyses in virtually every domain of science, and R integrates seamlessly with reproducible document systems like Quarto and R Markdown. The Positron IDE provides an excellent development environment that makes working with R accessible and productive. R is introduced in Chapter 11, with data wrangling and graphics in Chapter 13 and Chapter 14.
Python
Python is a general-purpose programming language that has become the lingua franca of image analysis, machine learning, and instrument control, and it is the language you are most likely to meet in code written by engineers outside the statistics community. R remains the primary language of this course, but Python gets a chapter of its own: you will install it in Chapter 2, and Chapter 12 covers the language, NumPy, pandas, and plotting at the same depth as Chapter 11, ending with a translation table between the two. You will also run Python code chunks in Quarto documents (Chapter 5) and use Python environments (venv, uv, and conda) both on your laptop and on Talapas. The concepts you learn in Bash and R (variables, loops, functions, files) transfer directly, and many students find that once R is comfortable, Python follows quickly.
Editors and IDEs (VS Code, Positron, RStudio)
All of the code in this course lives in plain-text files, and you will spend most of your working hours in the program that edits them. An integrated development environment (IDE) bundles a text editor with a terminal, a console for interactive R or Python, a file explorer, and a front-end to version control. We use three: VS Code, a general-purpose editor with the largest extension ecosystem; Positron, Posit’s data-science IDE built on the same open-source core as VS Code with R and Python built in; and RStudio, the classic R environment. Chapter 2 walks through installing and using each one and offers guidance on which to choose for which task.
Quarto and Reproducible Documents
Quarto is an open-source scientific publishing system (Posit Software, PBC, 2024) that enables you to combine narrative text with executable code in a single document. From this unified source, you can generate reports, presentations, websites, and books—all while ensuring your analyses are fully reproducible. Because the code runs when the document renders, results always match the code that produced them. You can then share your work in multiple formats (HTML, PDF, Word) without maintaining separate versions. This book itself was written using Quarto! See Chapter 5.
Git and GitHub
Git is a version control system that tracks changes to your files over time (Blischak et al., 2016; Chacon & Straub, 2014). GitHub is a web-based platform for hosting Git repositories. Together, they provide a complete history of your project’s development, allowing you to understand how your work evolved and revert to earlier versions if needed. Git enables safe experimentation with new ideas through branching—you can try risky changes without affecting your working code. The platform facilitates collaboration with colleagues worldwide, letting multiple people work on the same project simultaneously. And GitHub makes it easy to share code and data publicly, contributing to open science and reproducible research. Git and GitHub are covered in Chapter 20, with a command reference in Appendix I.
High-Performance Computing
Talapas is the University of Oregon’s computing cluster. You’ll learn to access and navigate this remote computing environment, submit and manage batch jobs that run when resources become available, use software modules to access specialized tools, and scale your analyses far beyond what your laptop can handle. When your analysis takes hours or days, or requires more memory than your personal computer has, Talapas provides the computational power you need (Chapter 16).

title: 1  Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
1.5 The Course Dataset
Most examples in the lectures use one small, real dataset so that each new tool is applied to data you already know. Stickle_RNAseq.tsv holds RNA-seq read counts for 600 genes measured in the guts of 80 threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) from the Cresko Lab. The fish come from two host genotypes (A and B) and were raised with either a conventional microbiota or a single bacterial species (“mono”), giving four groups of 20. The file is plain text, tab-separated, with one row per fish and columns Individual, Genotype, Microbiota, Geno&Micro, and Gene1 through Gene600.
You will count its rows at the shell (Chapter 7), pull out groups with grep, cut, and awk (Chapter 9), read it into R and Python (Chapter 11, Chapter 12), reshape and plot it (Chapter 13, Chapter 14), run the analysis as a batch job on Talapas (Chapter 16), and write it up as a Quarto report (Chapter 5). Download it once into your course project folder:
mkdir -p ~/projects/comptools/data
curl -L -o ~/projects/comptools/data/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv \
  https://wcresko.github.io/BioE_Comp_Tools_Fa2026/Data_Folder/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv

title: 1  Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
1.6 Setting Up Your Computing Environment
Before diving into the technical content, you’ll need to set up your computing environment. This section covers the operating-system level: getting a Unix shell on macOS, Linux, or Windows. The rest of the toolkit (R, Python, Quarto and TinyTeX, VS Code, and Positron) is installed in Chapter 2, which also has a verification checkpoint and a troubleshooting table; Git is installed in Chapter 20.
macOS Users
macOS is built on a Unix operating system, so a shell is already there. Open Terminal (in Applications → Utilities, or press Cmd-Space and type “Terminal”); if you prefer a more feature-rich terminal, iTerm2 is a popular alternative. One extra step is needed: install Apple’s command-line developer tools, which provide the compilers and Git that many other tools depend on. In Terminal, type
xcode-select --install
and click Install in the dialog that appears. It can take five to ten minutes; if the command reports that the tools are already installed, you are done. (Installing the full Xcode from the App Store also works, but it is many gigabytes and unnecessary for this course.) You can confirm the tools are in place with xcode-select -p, which prints their location, or simply git --version.






TipOptional: Homebrew



macOS has no built-in package manager for command-line software. Homebrew (https://brew.sh) fills that gap: once installed, brew install <name> fetches and installs tools such as wget, tree, or a newer git with one command, and brew update && brew upgrade keeps them current. Install it by pasting the single command shown on the Homebrew home page into Terminal (it needs the Xcode command-line tools, which you just installed). It is not required for this course, but later chapters mention it as one way to install Git (Chapter 20), and you will find that most macOS instructions on the web assume you have it.


Linux Users
Linux systems include multiple terminal applications. Open your distribution’s default terminal emulator, often called “Terminal” or “Console” (frequently Ctrl-Alt-T). Everything else in this chapter’s setup is already present; the only additions you will need are the compiler toolchain and R itself, both of which come from your package manager (sudo apt install build-essential gfortran r-base r-base-dev on Ubuntu/Debian) as described in Chapter 2.
Windows Users
Windows requires additional setup to access a Unix-like environment. The recommended approach uses Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), which runs a real Ubuntu Linux inside Windows. It requires Windows 11 or an up-to-date Windows 10.






CautionWindows Users: Additional Steps Required



Follow these steps to install Ubuntu on Windows:

Right-click Windows PowerShell (or Terminal) in the Start menu and choose Run as administrator

Type wsl --install and press Enter. This installs WSL and Ubuntu; there is no separate Ubuntu download. (If Ubuntu does not appear after the restart, run wsl --install -d Ubuntu, or install Ubuntu from the Microsoft Store)
When it finishes, restart your computer
Open Ubuntu from the Start menu and wait while it finishes installing
Create a Linux username and password. They do not need to match your Windows login, but remember them. When you type the password, nothing appears on screen; that is normal, so type it and press Enter
Update Ubuntu’s software (you will be asked for your Linux password):

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y


The Ubuntu window is a real Linux system, not PowerShell: it has its own home directory (/home/yourname, also written ~), its own files, and the Unix commands used throughout this book. Keep your course folders and files there. Your Windows files are visible from Ubuntu at /mnt/c/Users/<name> (for example /mnt/c/Users/<name>/Documents). Having two operating systems on one laptop is confusing at first; Chapter 2 has a “which side am I on?” table (Table 2.5) explaining where to type shell commands (Ubuntu) and where to install R, Python, and the IDEs (Windows). A detailed guide is available at ubuntu.com/tutorials/install-ubuntu-on-wsl2-on-windows-10, and Microsoft’s own instructions are at learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/install.






NoteIf WSL will not install



wsl --install needs hardware virtualization turned on and a reasonably current Windows. If it fails, run Windows Update, enable virtualization (often called VT-x, AMD-V, or SVM) in your computer’s BIOS/UEFI settings, and try again with wsl --update followed by wsl --install -d Ubuntu. On a laptop managed by a lab or department where this is not possible, Git Bash (installed with Git for Windows from https://git-scm.com/download/win) provides the basic Unix commands used in Chapter 4 and is enough to follow along, though not everything later in the book (package managers, Talapas-style scripts) will work there. Talk to the instructor early if you end up on this path.


Talapas Access
To use the university’s computing cluster, you must be a member of a PIRG (Principal Investigator Research Group), which your PI requests and manages; your login credentials are your Duck ID and password, with Duo two-step login. The UO VPN is recommended but not required: without it, you connect to login.talapas.uoregon.edu, a load balancer that spreads users across the login nodes; with it, you may also connect to a specific login node (login1 through login4) directly. Chapter 3 explains accounts, PIRGs, and the browser-based Open OnDemand interface, and Chapter 16 covers SSH and job submission in detail.

title: 1  Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
1.7 Course Structure and Expectations
This book is designed to accompany a hands-on course where most of class time is devoted to coding practice rather than lectures. Expect to:

Follow along with examples during class sessions
Complete practice exercises to reinforce concepts
Submit homework assignments demonstrating your skills
Develop a final project applying what you’ve learned to your own research







ImportantLearning Takes Practice



Computational skills develop through repeated practice. Don’t be discouraged if concepts don’t click immediately—everyone struggles at first. The key is persistence and willingness to experiment.

title: 1  Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
1.8 Getting Help
When you encounter problems (and you will!), several resources are available:
Manual Pages. Unix commands have built-in documentation accessible via man command_name. Type q to exit (see Section 4.3.1).
Help Functions. In R, use ?function_name or help(function_name) to access documentation.
The Internet. Sites like Stack Overflow contain solutions to virtually every common error message. Learning to search effectively is a crucial skill.
Generative AI. Tools like ChatGPT and Claude can explain concepts, debug code, and suggest solutions. However, always verify AI-generated code and understand what it does before using it. Chapter 19 discusses AI assistants, including those built into your editor, in depth.
UO Resources. The University provides a great deal of help of its own, from the Technology Service Desk to free R and Python consultations at UO Libraries and the RACS team behind Talapas; Chapter 3 lists them and explains how to ask a question that gets a fast answer.





Figure 1.1: Discriminative models predict labels from features by learning decision boundaries, while generative models learn the underlying probability distributions of data to generate new content. Understanding this distinction helps you choose the right AI tool for your task.


Each Other. Your classmates are experiencing the same learning curve. Collaboration and discussion accelerate everyone’s learning.

title: 1  Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
1.9 Summary
This chapter introduced the rationale for learning computational tools and provided an overview of the skills you’ll develop. Key takeaways:

Computational literacy is essential for modern biological research
Scripting languages (Bash, R, Python) are ideal for data analysis; this book teaches R in depth and Python alongside it
Version control and reproducibility are professional best practices
Learning requires patience, practice, and willingness to make mistakes

In Chapter 6, we’ll explore computer systems architecture to build your mental model of how computers work—knowledge that will inform everything that follows.

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
2.1 Why an Editor or IDE?
In Chapter 1 you set up the operating-system level of your computer: a Unix shell on macOS or Linux, or Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) with Ubuntu on Windows. This chapter fills in the rest of the toolkit. By the end you should have the languages we use (R and Python), the publishing system that turns code and prose into documents (Quarto, with a small LaTeX distribution for PDFs), and, most importantly, a comfortable place to write and run code: an editor or IDE.
We spend far more time in this chapter on the editor than on any single language. That is deliberate. Over the course of a graduate degree you will spend hundreds of hours writing scripts, documents, and analyses, and almost all of that time is spent inside an editor. Learning its layout, shortcuts, and quirks early is the single best productivity investment you can make.
Every program you write in this course, whether a Bash script, an R analysis, or a Quarto document, is a plain-text file. In principle you could write it with any tool that produces plain text, and for quick edits on a remote server, terminal editors such as nano and vim remain useful (we will meet them in Chapter 4). But plain editors do not scale to real projects. Once your work spans a dozen files across several directories, you want a tool that can show the whole project at once, that color-codes your code so structure and mistakes are visible at a glance, and that lets you run code right where you write it.
An Integrated Development Environment (IDE) bundles those capabilities into one window: a text editor with syntax highlighting and completion, a terminal for shell commands, a console for an interactive R or Python session, and tools such as a file explorer, a search across the project, and an interface to version control (Chapter 20). The three IDEs you will encounter in this course, VS Code, Positron, and RStudio, all provide these pieces; they differ mainly in emphasis, as we discuss in Section 2.7.

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
TipOpen the folder, not the file



All three IDEs work best when they can see your entire project. Always use File → Open Folder (or its equivalent) on the project’s top-level directory, rather than double-clicking a single file. The file explorer then shows the whole tree, project-wide search works, and the integrated terminal opens in that folder automatically, so relative paths in your scripts behave as expected.
crumbs: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
2.2 Is Your Laptop Ready?
Before installing anything, make sure your machine can handle the software. The course requires a laptop with 16 GB of RAM (8 GB is the absolute minimum and will struggle with larger datasets later in the term), at least 20 GB of free disk space (the installs in this chapter alone take roughly 10 GB, and your data needs room too), and an up-to-date macOS, Windows 10/11, or Linux. You also need administrator rights to install software; if your laptop is managed by a lab or department, you may need to ask their IT staff for help. Chromebooks and iPads will not work for this course. If you do not have a suitable laptop, talk to the instructor early so that a solution can be found.
Some installers, R in particular, come in different versions for different processors, so it helps to know what kind of chip you have. Table 2.1 shows how to find out.



Table 2.1: Finding out which processor your computer has










System
How to check
What you will see




macOS
Apple menu → About This Mac
Chip: Apple M1/M2/M3/M4 (Apple silicon) or Processor: Intel


Windows
Settings → System → About
Processor, RAM, “64-bit operating system”


Any Unix shell
uname -m
arm64 (Apple silicon or other ARM) or x86_64 (Intel/AMD)






While you are there, note your RAM and free disk space. In Chapter 3 we compare these numbers to what a single node of the Talapas cluster offers; the comparison is instructive.

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
2.3 The Install Checklist
Here is everything you need to install for the course, in a sensible order. Several of the downloads are large, so it is worth starting them and letting them run while you read the rest of the chapter. The operating-system prerequisites (the Xcode command-line tools on macOS, and WSL with Ubuntu on Windows) are covered in Chapter 1; make sure those are finished first.

A Unix shell
On macOS and Linux you already have one: open Terminal (on macOS, press Cmd-Space and type “Terminal”; on Linux, often Ctrl-Alt-T). On Windows, the shell you will use for this course is the Ubuntu app installed by WSL. Confirm it works by typing echo $SHELL and whoami at the prompt. macOS uses zsh by default and Ubuntu uses bash; for everything in this course they behave the same.


R
Download R from CRAN at https://cran.r-project.org. Install R before Positron or RStudio, since both look for an existing R when they first start. On macOS, click “Download R for macOS” and choose the .pkg installer that matches your chip: arm64 for Apple silicon (M1 through M4) or x86_64 for Intel Macs. If you are unsure, run uname -m in Terminal (Table 2.1). Open the downloaded file and follow the prompts; R ends up in your Applications folder. On Windows, click “Download R for Windows”, then “base”, then the link for the latest version; run the .exe installer, accepting the defaults, and R appears in the Start menu. On Linux (Ubuntu/Debian), install from the package manager and confirm the version in one go:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y r-base r-base-dev
R --version
Other distributions have their own instructions on the CRAN site. Whichever platform you are on, a quick check that R itself works is to start it and type R.version.string; it should print something like R version 4.5.1 (2025-06-13). R is the subject of Chapter 11 and everything that follows it.






NoteWindows: install R and Python on the Windows side



If you use WSL, install R, Python, VS Code, and Positron as ordinary Windows applications, not inside Ubuntu. The IDEs run on Windows and will find the Windows copies of R and Python; Ubuntu is where you will type shell commands. Section 2.8 explains how to tell the two apart.




Python
There are three common ways to install Python 3, and for this course any of them is fine as long as you pick one and stick with it:

The python.org installer (simplest). Download from https://www.python.org/downloads/. On macOS, run the installer. On Windows, the first screen of the installer has a checkbox labeled “Add python.exe to PATH”: check it. If you skip it, your terminal will not be able to find Python and you will end up reinstalling.
uv (fastest). A single small program from https://docs.astral.sh/uv/ that installs Python versions, creates environments, and installs packages; uv python install 3.12 fetches an interpreter.
conda (Miniconda or Miniforge). A package manager that also installs non-Python software; it is the standard on Talapas and in bioinformatics, but heavier than the other two.

Inside Ubuntu on WSL, Python is already present, but the tools for installing packages and creating environments are not, so add them with:
sudo apt install -y python3-pip python3-venv
The trade-offs among these options, and how to use environments with each, are covered in Chapter 12.


Quarto
Quarto turns Markdown and code into HTML pages, PDFs, Word documents, and slides; it is how this book and the course slides are built. Download the installer for your operating system from https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/ and run it. Quarto is covered in depth in Chapter 5.


TinyTeX
To produce PDFs, Quarto needs a LaTeX distribution, the standard system for typesetting mathematics (Chapter 18). Full distributions such as MacTeX and MiKTeX are several gigabytes; TinyTeX installs only what Quarto needs. After Quarto is installed, open a terminal and run:
quarto --version
quarto install tinytex     # takes several minutes
If you already have a full LaTeX distribution, Quarto will find and use it, and you can skip this step.
TinyTeX can also be installed from inside R, which is convenient if you have an R console open and have not yet opened a terminal. In the R console:
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()     # takes several minutes; restart the IDE afterwards
Either route produces the same TinyTeX; do not run both. TinyTeX installs additional LaTeX packages automatically the first time a document needs them, which is why it stays small. If you would rather have a complete distribution, the standard choices are MacTeX (https://www.tug.org/mactex/, about 4 GB) on macOS, MiKTeX (https://miktex.org/download; say yes to automatic package installation) on Windows, and sudo apt install texlive texlive-latex-extra texlive-fonts-recommended on Ubuntu/Debian (texlive-full if disk space is no object).
To confirm that a LaTeX engine is available, run quarto check in a terminal and look for the “LaTeX” line, or in R:
tinytex::is_tinytex()          # TRUE if TinyTeX is installed
Sys.which("pdflatex")          # path to the engine (empty if none is found)


VS Code
Download Visual Studio Code from https://code.visualstudio.com/download. It is free and requires no account. Run the installer, open VS Code, and allow any permissions it asks for. Installation details and the extensions we use are in Section 2.4.


Positron
Download Positron from https://positron.posit.co/download. Install R and Python before Positron so that it can find them automatically. Details are in Section 2.5.


RStudio
RStudio Desktop is Posit’s classic, R-focused IDE. It is optional for this course but worth having if you already know it, and it is the environment you will meet on Talapas through Open OnDemand (Chapter 3). Download the free open-source edition from https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/; the page detects your operating system and offers the right installer. On macOS, open the .dmg and drag RStudio to your Applications folder; on Windows, run the installer with the defaults; on Ubuntu, download the .deb and install it with sudo apt install ./rstudio-*.deb. Install R first: RStudio finds it automatically when it starts. Details are in Section 2.6.


Compiler tools
Several R and Python packages (and nearly all Bioconductor packages) compile from source the first time you install them, which requires a working C, C++, and often Fortran compiler. Install the toolchain once now; Section 2.13 lists the errors you will see if it is missing.
macOS. Apple’s Xcode command-line tools, installed in Chapter 1 with xcode-select --install, provide clang, git, and make. They do not include a Fortran compiler, which some R packages need; if you ever see gfortran not found, install gfortran from the R for macOS tools page at https://mac.r-project.org/tools/, then relaunch your IDE.
Windows. Install Rtools from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/, choosing the version that matches your R (for example Rtools44 for R 4.4, Rtools45 for R 4.5). Rtools is for the Windows copy of R; it is separate from Ubuntu on WSL, which uses build-essential as described next.
Linux (including Ubuntu on WSL). Install the toolchain from the package manager:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y build-essential gfortran
build-essential provides gcc, g++, and make; gfortran covers packages with Fortran code. On Fedora or RHEL, use sudo dnf groupinstall "Development Tools" and add gcc-gfortran.


Git (later)
We will also use Git for version control, but not yet. Installing and configuring Git, and connecting it to GitHub, is done in Chapter 20, so there is nothing to do now.

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
2.4 Visual Studio Code
VS Code is a free, general-purpose code editor from Microsoft, built on the open-source Code OSS project. It runs on macOS, Windows, and Linux, supports essentially every programming language through extensions, and has the largest extension ecosystem and user community of any editor. It is also the editor most likely to be waiting for you on a collaborator’s machine or in a company.

Installing and opening a project
After running the installer from https://code.visualstudio.com/download, open VS Code and use File → Open Folder to open your project directory. Windows users will be prompted to install the WSL extension; accept, because it allows VS Code to work directly inside Ubuntu. Once the WSL extension is installed, typing code . in an Ubuntu terminal opens the current directory in VS Code, connected to Ubuntu.
On macOS, the code command is not on your PATH by default. Open the Command Palette (Cmd-Shift-P), type “shell command”, and run “Shell Command: Install ‘code’ command in PATH”. From then on, code . in Terminal opens the current folder, and code somefile.R opens a single file.


The layout
VS Code’s window has a handful of regions that you will use constantly. The Activity Bar runs down the far left and switches the side panel between the Explorer (a file tree of your open folder), Search (find text across the entire project), Source Control (a graphical front-end to Git, covered in Chapter 20), and Extensions. The editor occupies the center; you can open many files in tabs and split the editor to see two files side by side with Cmd-\ (macOS) or Ctrl-\ (Windows/Linux). The integrated terminal at the bottom is a full shell (zsh, bash, or, on Windows with the WSL extension, Ubuntu’s bash); toggle it with Ctrl-`, the backtick key that sits above Tab. Finally, the Command Palette, opened with Cmd-Shift-P or Ctrl-Shift-P, lets you find and run any command by typing part of its name. If you cannot remember where a menu item lives, the Command Palette is the answer.


Extensions for this course
Open the Extensions panel (Cmd-Shift-X / Ctrl-Shift-X), search for each of the following, and click Install:

Quarto (from Quarto), to edit, preview, and render .qmd documents
Python (from Microsoft), for Python language support
R (from REditorSupport), for R language support
Jupyter (from Microsoft), for notebooks and interactive Python
WSL (from Microsoft; Windows only), to work inside Ubuntu
Later in the term, Remote - SSH (from Microsoft), which lets you edit files on Talapas as if they were local (Chapter 16)

Extensions can be added and removed at any time, so start with this short list and add more as you discover a need.


Keyboard shortcuts worth memorizing
A few shortcuts account for most of the time savings in an editor. Table 2.2 lists the ones worth learning first; they work identically in Positron. A fuller list, including shell shortcuts, is in Appendix A.

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
2.5 Positron
Positron is a free, next-generation data-science IDE from Posit. It is built on Code OSS, the open-source core of VS Code, so everything in the previous section (Explorer, editor tabs, terminal, Command Palette, the shortcuts in Table 2.2) carries over unchanged. What Positron adds is a set of data-science panes and native support for both R and Python.

Installing
Download Positron from https://positron.posit.co/download and run the installer. Because Positron discovers the R and Python installations on your computer when it starts, install both languages first. Then open Positron, use File → Open Folder on your project, and start an R or Python session from the interpreter picker at the top right of the window. You can have several sessions open and switch among them, which is convenient for projects that mix R and Python.


The layout
In addition to the VS Code regions, Positron adds a Console, an interactive R or Python session where you can type expressions and see results immediately; a Variables pane listing every object you have created, with its type and size; a Plots pane that displays your figures and keeps a history of them; a Data Explorer that opens a data frame in a spreadsheet-like, sortable, filterable view; and a Help pane showing documentation for the function under your cursor. The recommended workflow: write code in the editor, where it is saved in a file, and send lines or selections to the console with Cmd-Enter (macOS) or Ctrl-Enter (Windows/Linux). Use the console directly only for quick experiments; anything you would want to reproduce belongs in a file.


Extensions in Positron
Positron installs extensions from Open VSX, an open extension registry, rather than from Microsoft’s Visual Studio Marketplace. Most extensions you would want (Quarto, Python, Jupyter, and many others) are available there, but a few Microsoft-only extensions are not, and Positron provides its own equivalents for the important ones. In particular, the VS Code R extension is not used in Positron: R support is built in, so do not install it.
crumbs: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
2.6 RStudio
RStudio, also from Posit, is the IDE that most R users learned on, and it remains an excellent environment for pure R work. Its window is divided into four fixed panes: the Source editor (top-left) for scripts and Quarto documents; the Console (bottom-left) for a live R session; the Environment/History pane (top-right) listing your objects and past commands; and the Files/Plots/Packages/Help/Viewer pane (bottom-right). The workflow is the same as in Positron: write in the Source pane and send lines to the Console with Cmd-Enter / Ctrl-Enter. RStudio has Quarto rendering built in (the Render button, Cmd/Ctrl-Shift-K), an RStudio Projects system (.Rproj files) that sets the working directory for you (Section 11.2.2), and a Tools → Install Packages dialog. It runs Python through the reticulate package but is not designed for it, and it has no general extension marketplace, so this course uses it for R work only.

section: 2.7 VS Code vs. Positron vs. RStudio: Which Should I Use?
text:
2.7 VS Code vs. Positron vs. RStudio: Which Should I Use?
Because Positron is built on Code OSS, VS Code and Positron share their editor, Command Palette, terminal, keyboard shortcuts, settings format, and Quarto support; both are free, cross-platform, support extensions, and can connect to remote machines over SSH. The difference is focus. Positron is built for data science: R and Python are first-class, and the Console, Variables, Plots, and Data Explorer panes are always at hand. VS Code is general-purpose: any language works through extensions, its extension library and community are the largest, and it is the tool of choice for shell scripts, configuration files, and polyglot projects. title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
section: 2.8 Windows: Which Side Am I On?
text:
2.8 Windows: Which Side Am I On?
With WSL installed, a Windows laptop effectively runs two operating systems: Windows itself and Ubuntu. Both are useful, but it matters which one you are typing into, because they have different home directories, different views of the file system, and different commands. Table 2.5 is the map.



Table 2.5: Windows and Ubuntu on the same laptop











Windows side
Ubuntu (WSL) side




Terminal
PowerShell or Command Prompt
The Ubuntu app, or a VS Code terminal showing “WSL: Ubuntu”


Prompt looks like
PS C:\Users\you>
you@laptop:~$


Your home folder
C:\Users\you
/home/you (also ~)


The other side’s files
\\wsl$\Ubuntu\home\you
/mnt/c/Users/you


Unix commands (ls, grep, …)
Mostly no
Yes


Where R, Python, VS Code, Positron are installed
Here
(not needed)






The rule for this course is simple: type shell commands in Ubuntu, and install R, Python, VS Code, and Positron on the Windows side. In VS Code, a green badge in the bottom-left corner reading WSL: Ubuntu tells you that the window is connected to Ubuntu; without it, the integrated terminal is PowerShell and Unix commands will mostly fail. Your Linux home directory (/home/you) lives on a virtual disk and is the fastest place to work; your Windows files are reachable from Ubuntu under /mnt/c/ (for example /mnt/c/Users/you/Documents), and Ubuntu’s files appear in Windows File Explorer under Linux in the sidebar, or at the path \\wsl$\Ubuntu\home\you. Installing Windows Terminal from the Microsoft Store gives you a nicer terminal with tabs that can open either side.






TipKeep projects in the Linux home directory



WSL and Windows share files, so you never need two copies of anything, but where a project lives affects speed. Working inside the Linux home directory (~, that is /home/you) is noticeably faster than working under /mnt/c, and case-sensitivity rules differ between the two file systems. Keep course projects in your Linux home and reach over to /mnt/c/Users/you/Downloads only when you need a file that arrived on the Windows side. If you later run R or Python inside Ubuntu, keep the project under ~/ as well; running a WSL program on files under /mnt/c is the most common cause of mysteriously slow file reading.

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
2.9 Jupyter Notebooks vs. Quarto Documents
Two file formats let you mix code, its output, and explanatory text in one document, and you will encounter both. A Jupyter notebook (.ipynb) is made of cells, each containing code or Markdown, and the outputs are saved inside the file alongside the code. Notebooks are enormously popular in Python, machine learning, and image analysis; they run in JupyterLab, VS Code, and Positron, and on Talapas through Open OnDemand (Chapter 3). Their drawback is that the file is stored as JSON with embedded output, which makes it hard to read as text and awkward to track in Git.
A Quarto document (.qmd) is plain text: Markdown prose with a YAML header and code chunks in R, Python, Julia, or Bash. Output is not stored in the source; it is regenerated every time you render, which is exactly what reproducibility demands, and the plain-text source is easy to read, edit, and diff in Git. Quarto renders to HTML, PDF, Word, slides, and websites (Chapter 5). You do not have to choose between the two: Quarto can render Jupyter notebooks directly with quarto render notebook.ipynb, and can use Jupyter as the engine for Python chunks in .qmd files. This course uses Quarto; many of your labs may use Jupyter, and the skills transfer.
crumbs: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
2.10 A Preview of Python Environments
Different projects need different versions of packages, and installing everything into one Python installation eventually breaks something. The solution is an environment: an isolated set of packages for one project. Python’s built-in venv module creates one in your project folder:
python3 -m venv .venv            # create an environment in this project
source .venv/bin/activate        # turn it on (Windows PowerShell: .venv\Scripts\activate)
pip install numpy pandas         # install packages into it
deactivate                       # turn it off
While the environment is active, python and pip refer to the copies inside .venv, and packages you install go there rather than into the system Python. On Talapas you will instead use conda environments, which can manage non-Python software as well (Chapter 16); uv is a fast, modern alternative to venv and pip; and R has the same idea in the renv package. There is nothing to set up now; the point is to know the word “environment” so that it is not a surprise later.
crumbs: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
2.11 AI Assistants Inside the Editor
Both IDEs can host an AI coding assistant. GitHub Copilot in VS Code suggests code as you type and answers questions in a chat panel; it is free for verified students through the GitHub Student Developer Pack. Positron Assistant is an AI chat built into Positron that can see your console, variables, and plots. Both are genuinely useful for explaining error messages, writing boilerplate, and learning unfamiliar syntax.
They are also confidently wrong surprisingly often. Treat every suggestion as a draft from a well-read but careless colleague: read it, run it, and make sure you understand it before it goes into your analysis. Never paste sensitive data (see the data-classification rules in Chapter 3) into an assistant, and follow the course’s AI policy: you may use these tools to learn and debug, but the work you submit must be your own. We return to AI-assisted coding, and how to use it well, in Chapter 19; there is no need to set anything up now.
crumbs: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
2.12 Verification Checkpoint
Once everything is installed, open a terminal inside VS Code or Positron (Ctrl-`) and run the following commands:
echo $SHELL
R --version
python3 --version     # Windows PowerShell (not WSL): try  py --version
quarto --version
quarto check          # checks for R, Python, and LaTeX
Each should print a version number (or, for quarto check, a list of passing checks), not “command not found.” Then open Positron and confirm that you can start both an R console and a Python console from the interpreter picker; in the R console, sessionInfo() prints the R version, platform, and loaded packages in one place, which is exactly what you will be asked for when reporting a problem. The most complete end-to-end test is to create a new Quarto document (in VS Code or Positron, Command Palette → Quarto: New Document), set format: pdf in its header, and render it: that exercises Quarto, the language engine, and TinyTeX at once. If a command is not found, the most likely explanation is that the terminal was opened before the program was installed: a terminal only sees programs that were on the PATH when it started, so close and reopen the terminal, or restart the IDE, before doing anything else. Table 2.6 lists other common problems.

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
2.13 Troubleshooting Common Setup Problems
Table 2.6 covers the problems that appear while installing. The following come up a little later, usually the first time you install R packages or start a real project, and every one of them has bitten several students in past years.

macOS: “compilation failed” or clang errors when installing a package
The Xcode command-line tools are missing or out of date. In Terminal:
xcode-select --install
Relaunch Positron or RStudio after the install finishes. If the error instead mentions gfortran not found or library not found for -lgfortran, install gfortran from https://mac.r-project.org/tools/ (see the compiler tools item in Section 2.3) and try the package install again.


Windows: “WARNING: Rtools is required to build R packages”
R is trying to compile a package but cannot find Rtools, or you have an Rtools version that does not match your R version (Rtools44 for R 4.4, and so on). Install the matching version from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/, restart R, and confirm with Sys.which("make"), which should now print a path.


BiocManager::install() hangs or takes forever on one package
The most common cause is a slow Bioconductor mirror. Pick a closer one and try again:
chooseBioCmirror()                              # interactive; pick a US mirror
options(BioC_mirror = "https://bioconductor.org")
BiocManager::install("DESeq2")
The first Bioconductor install compiles many dependencies and can genuinely take 20 to 60 minutes; do it the day before you need it, not the morning of.


Positron or RStudio “can’t find” a package you just installed
Almost always a stale R session: the package was installed, but the running session was started before. Restart R (Session → Restart R, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + F10) and try library() again. If that does not help, the package may have been installed into the library of a different R version than the one the IDE is running:
.libPaths()                          # which library folders is this session using?
installed.packages()[, "Package"]    # what is actually installed there?
R.version.string                     # which R is this?
If the versions do not match, point the IDE at the correct R install (Positron: the interpreter picker at the top right; RStudio: Tools → Global Options → General → R version) and reinstall the package there.


Windows/WSL: R or Python is painfully slow, or cannot see the project files
The project is on the Windows side (/mnt/c/Users/...) but the program is running inside WSL, or the reverse. File access across that boundary is dramatically slower, and case-sensitivity differs. Choose one arrangement and stick with it: either run R, Python, and the IDE as Windows programs with the project under C:\Users\you, which is what this course recommends (Section 2.8), or run everything inside Ubuntu with the project under ~/.


Rendering to PDF fails, or LaTeX complains about a missing .sty file
Quarto rendered your document to HTML without complaint, but format: pdf stops with an error. Read the end of the log: the message usually names the problem. If it is ! LaTeX Error: File 'something.sty' not found, TinyTeX normally installs the missing package on the fly; when it does not (typically because the package index is stale), update TinyTeX and install the package by hand, using either the terminal or the R console:
quarto update tinytex          # refresh TinyTeX and its package index
tlmgr install <package-name>   # e.g. tlmgr install fontawesome5
tinytex::tlmgr_update()
tinytex::tlmgr_install("package-name")
If quarto check reports that no LaTeX installation was found at all, TinyTeX is not installed or not on your PATH: run quarto install tinytex again (Section 2.3.5) and reopen the terminal. If the TinyTeX installer itself hangs, the usual culprit is a firewall or a campus network that blocks the CTAN mirror; try again from a different network.


Old results keep coming back after a fix
R keeps every object you create for the whole session, so a later chunk can silently use an old object after you edit an earlier one. Restart R and run the script from the top; rm(list = ls()) clears variables but not loaded packages, so a restart is more reliable. Do not save the workspace to .RData on exit (answer “no” if R asks; in RStudio, set Tools → Global Options → General → Save workspace to Never), so that each session starts clean.
crumbs: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
2.14 Keeping Software Updated
Nothing in this chapter is install-once-and-forget. New versions bring bug fixes, security patches, and, in the case of R, access to packages that require a recent version. Once a term is a reasonable rhythm, and Table 2.7 lists how each piece is updated. Two cautions: do not update the morning of a deadline, and after a major R upgrade (for example 4.4 to 4.5) expect to reinstall your packages, because each major version keeps its own package library.



Table 2.7: Updating the course toolkit





Tool
How to update




R
Download and run the current installer from CRAN (Linux: sudo apt upgrade); then reinstall packages if the major version changed


R packages
In R: update.packages(ask = FALSE)


RStudio
Help → Check for Updates, or download the current installer


VS Code, Positron
Both check for updates automatically; Help → Check for Updates (or Code → Check for Updates on macOS) forces it


Python (python.org)
Run the newer installer; uv self update if you use uv; conda update conda for conda


Python packages
Inside the environment: pip install --upgrade <package> (or uv pip install --upgrade)


Quarto
Download and run the current installer from https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/


TinyTeX
quarto update tinytex in a terminal, or tinytex::tlmgr_update() in R


macOS command-line tools and Homebrew
System Settings → Software Update handles Xcode tools; brew update && brew upgrade for Homebrew packages


Ubuntu (including WSL)
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade


WSL itself
In PowerShell: wsl --update






After any update, run the checkpoint commands in Section 2.12 again; a surprising number of “it worked yesterday” problems are a tool that updated itself overnight and now needs the terminal reopened or a package reinstalled.
crumbs: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
2.15 Summary
This chapter assembled the software you will use for the rest of the course and, more importantly, introduced the place where you will do most of your work: the editor. Key takeaways:

An IDE combines an editor, terminal, console, and project tools in one window; always open the whole project folder, not a single file
The core installs are R (matching your chip), Python (with “Add to PATH” on Windows), Quarto with TinyTeX, VS Code, and Positron; Git comes later in Chapter 20
VS Code is general-purpose with the largest ecosystem; Positron is built on the same core with R and Python and data-science panes built in; RStudio remains a fine choice for pure R
On Windows, type shell commands in Ubuntu but install languages and IDEs on the Windows side, and watch for the “WSL: Ubuntu” badge
Quarto documents are plain text and regenerate their output; Jupyter notebooks store output in the file; Quarto can render both
Python environments (venv, conda, uv) and R’s renv isolate each project’s packages
Editor-based AI assistants are useful for learning and debugging but must be read, tested, and never fed sensitive data
Compiling packages needs a toolchain: Xcode command-line tools plus gfortran on macOS, Rtools matching your R version on Windows, build-essential gfortran on Linux
R --version, python3 --version, quarto --version, and quarto check confirm a working installation; when a command is not found, reopen the terminal first
The most common later problems (compiler errors, slow Bioconductor mirrors, a stale R session, missing LaTeX packages, projects on the wrong side of WSL) are collected in Section 2.13
Update the toolkit once a term (Table 2.7), never the morning of a deadline; a major R upgrade means reinstalling packages

In Chapter 3 we turn from your laptop to the resources the University provides: your digital identity, cloud storage, data-security rules, site-licensed software, and the Talapas cluster.
crumbs: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs

title: 2  Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
Exercises






TipPractice Exercises




Checkpoint: Run every command in Section 2.12 and record the version of R, Python, and Quarto on your machine. Note which shell echo $SHELL reports and whether quarto check finds LaTeX.
Project layout: Create a folder called bootcamp with subfolders data/raw, data/processed, scripts, output/figures, and docs. Open the folder in VS Code and in Positron. In each, open the integrated terminal and run pwd to confirm it started in your project directory.
Extensions: Install the Quarto, Python, R, and Jupyter extensions in VS Code (and, on Windows, WSL). Then open Positron’s Extensions panel and confirm that the Quarto extension is available from Open VSX. What happens if you search for the R extension there?
Shortcuts: In a new file, type three lines of code, select them, and use the toggle-comment shortcut from Table 2.2 to comment and uncomment them. Then use the project-wide search to find every occurrence of the word library in your bootcamp folder.
Windows only: Open a PowerShell window and an Ubuntu window side by side. In each, print your home directory (echo $HOME in Ubuntu; echo $HOME or $env:USERPROFILE in PowerShell) and list its contents. Then, from Ubuntu, ls /mnt/c/Users/<your name> and confirm you can see your Windows files.

title: 3  Computing Resources at the University of Oregon
text:
3.1 Your UO Digital Identity
The previous chapters equipped your laptop. This chapter is about everything the University of Oregon provides beyond your laptop: the accounts that unlock its services, the places where you can store and share files, the rules that govern what may go where, the software the University licenses on your behalf, and the research computing cluster, Talapas, that you will use later in the course. Much of this is mundane, but it is the kind of mundane that, ignored, costs people a thesis chapter, a data-security incident, or a week of waiting for a cluster account. An hour spent understanding it now is well invested.
Almost everything in this chapter begins with your Duck ID, the UO username and password that you manage at https://duckid.uoregon.edu. It is the key to email, Canvas, Microsoft 365, the software download site, and Talapas. Most UO services also require two-step login through Duo: after entering your password, you approve the login on a second device, usually the Duo Mobile app on your phone. Set Duo up before you need it; being unable to log in to a service you need in a hurry is a frustrating way to discover that your phone is not enrolled.
Your UO email address (you@uoregon.edu) doubles as your sign-in name for Microsoft 365 and for UO’s Dropbox contract. When a service asks you to “sign in with your work or school account,” this is the account it means.
The UO VPN, delivered through the Cisco Secure Client and downloadable from https://uovpn.uoregon.edu, makes your off-campus computer appear to be on the campus network. You only need it for campus-restricted resources such as some library databases, departmental file shares, and some licensed software that must be activated from the campus network. Most UO services, including email, Canvas, Microsoft 365, Teams, and Zoom, work from anywhere without it.

section: 3.2 Where to Get Help at UO
text:
3.2 Where to Get Help at UO
There is a lot of help available at UO, and a large part of getting unstuck quickly is knowing which door to knock on. The UO Service Portal at https://service.uoregon.edu is the front door for all campus technology: it has a searchable knowledge base and a ticketing system, and most questions about accounts, software, Wi-Fi, and cloud storage already have an article there, so search it first. Behind the portal sits the Technology Service Desk, reachable by phone at 541-346-4357 or through live chat.
For data analysis rather than technology, UO Libraries Data Services (https://library.uoregon.edu/data-services) is an underused treasure. They run free workshops on R, Python, data analysis, and related topics; offer one-on-one consultations, in person or on Zoom, on statistics, R, Python, version control, and data-management plans; and staff a drop-in help desk in Knight Library on weekdays from 11am to 4pm.
For research computing, RACS (Research Advanced Computing Services), which runs Talapas, can be reached at racs@uoregon.edu or through their service desk at https://hpcrcf.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/1; Section 3.10 describes what they do. Closer to home, the Center for Biomedical Data Science (CBDS) at the Knight Campus, directed by the author of this book, supports the computational and data-science side of biomedical research at the Knight Campus, including training such as this course; ask the instructor about CBDS resources and events. Your home department and the Knight Campus also have IT staff who can help with lab computers and shared storage.

How to ask for help well
Whoever you ask, the quality of the answer depends on the quality of the question. Start by saying what you were trying to do (“I’m trying to install R on my M2 Mac”), then include the exact error message as copied text, not a blurry photograph of your screen (a screenshot is acceptable only if the text cannot be copied). Show the command or code you ran and what you expected to happen, say what you have already tried (restarted? searched the error? checked your location with pwd?), and state your system: macOS, Windows, or Ubuntu, and the chip type. For code problems, reduce the problem to a minimal example, the smallest piece of code that still shows the failure. Half the time, the discipline of writing a good question leads you to the answer yourself; the other half, it lets someone else answer in a single reply.

text:
3.3 The Microsoft 365 Stack
Every UO student and employee has a Microsoft 365 license, which you access by signing in at https://office.uoregon.edu with your UO email address. Table 3.1 lists what it includes.



Table 3.1: The Microsoft 365 tools available to UO students and employees









Tool
What it is for




Outlook
UO email and calendar


Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OneNote
Desktop, web, and mobile apps; install them on your own devices from office.uoregon.edu


Teams
Chat, meetings, and shared files for groups and labs


OneDrive
Your personal cloud storage (1 TB)


SharePoint / Teams files
Shared storage owned by a group rather than a person


Copilot Chat
UO-protected generative AI assistant, when signed in with your UO account







OneDrive
OneDrive is your personal cloud storage, available at no cost with 1 TB of space. The OneDrive sync app for Mac and Windows creates a OneDrive folder on your computer, and files you save there are copied to the cloud automatically, so they survive a lost or dead laptop. You can share files and folders with UO colleagues and with outside collaborators. OneDrive is approved for FERPA and HIPAA data (see Section 3.4), and individual files may be as large as 250 GB.






WarningOneDrive is yours; lab data belongs in shared storage



OneDrive belongs to you, and when you leave UO it goes away. Data that belongs to a lab, such as raw experimental data, shared analysis code, and protocols, should live in storage the lab controls: a Teams/SharePoint site, a lab Dropbox team folder, or the lab’s project space on Talapas. Otherwise, it leaves when you do.




UO Dropbox
UO also holds an institutional Dropbox contract, but eligibility changed in 2026. Since March 2026, Dropbox accounts under the UO contract are available to faculty, staff, officers of administration, and graduate employees (GEs); students who are not UO employees no longer have access and should use OneDrive instead. If you are eligible, sign in with your UO email address and install the desktop app so that your files sync to a local folder; individual accounts have 2 TB of storage, and labs and departments can purchase team storage. Your lab may also share a Dropbox team folder with you regardless of whether you have your own account. Dropbox is approved for green and amber data, including FERPA records, but not for HIPAA or other red data.


Synced folders have real paths
Both OneDrive and Dropbox create an ordinary folder on your computer, which means it has a path you can use from the command line and from your scripts. Typical locations look like these (yours may differ slightly):
# macOS
~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-UniversityofOregon
~/University\ of\ Oregon\ Dropbox/Your\ Name

# Windows, as seen from Ubuntu/WSL
/mnt/c/Users/you/OneDrive\ -\ University\ of\ Oregon
Notice the backslashes: names such as University of Oregon Dropbox contain spaces, and the shell uses spaces to separate arguments, so a path with spaces must be quoted (cd "University of Oregon Dropbox") or escaped with backslashes. Tab completion adds the escapes for you, and Chapter 4 has more on paths and quoting. Find your own synced folder with cd, ls, and Tab completion. Synced folders are excellent for documents and drafts, but large or rapidly changing analysis files are better kept on local disk or on Talapas, where the sync client cannot interfere with them.

section: 3.4 Data Classification: What Can Go Where?
text:
3.4 Data Classification: What Can Go Where?
UO classifies data by the harm that would result if it were exposed, and the classification determines where it may be stored and which tools may touch it. Know the class of your data before you choose where to put it. Table 3.2 summarizes the three classes.



Table 3.2: UO’s data classification and where each class may live










Class
Examples
May be stored in




Green (low risk)
Published data, your code, most de-identified research data
Almost anywhere, including AI tools


Amber (medium risk)
FERPA student records, unpublished research data
OneDrive, Dropbox, Teams/SharePoint


Red (high risk)
HIPAA / protected health information, Social Security numbers, credit-card numbers
Only approved systems (for example OneDrive for HIPAA); ask first












Important



Only green data may be entered into AI tools that UO does not officially support. Microsoft Copilot Chat, signed in with your UO account, is approved for more; see Section 3.9.



Protecting research data
Two categories deserve special attention. Human-subjects data, meaning anything covered by an Institutional Review Board (IRB) protocol, and protected health information covered by HIPAA are red, high-risk data. Store them only where your IRB protocol and UO approve: UO OneDrive and Teams are approved for HIPAA data, Dropbox is not, and personal cloud accounts (a personal Google Drive or iCloud), email attachments, and unsupported AI tools are never acceptable. De-identify data as early in the workflow as you can, and keep the key that links identifiers to participants separately and securely. Encrypt your laptop (FileVault on macOS, BitLocker or Device Encryption on Windows) and use a screen lock, so that a stolen backpack is an inconvenience rather than a breach. Finally, remember that unpublished data and code are valuable; do not post them publicly until your PI agrees. When in doubt, ask before you store or share, whether your PI, the IRB, or the Service Portal. It is far easier than cleaning up afterwards.

title: 3  Computing Resources at the University of Oregon
text:
3.5 Backups and the 3-2-1 Rule
Every year, someone loses a thesis chapter to a dead laptop or a stolen bag. The standard defense is the 3-2-1 rule: keep three copies of anything important, on two different kinds of storage, with one copy off-site. In practice that might mean the working copy on your laptop, a versioned backup on an external drive using Time Machine (macOS) or File History (Windows), and an off-site copy in OneDrive or your lab’s Dropbox or server. For code, GitHub adds a fourth layer: every commit you push is a backup with full history (Chapter 20).






WarningA synced folder is not a backup



OneDrive and Dropbox protect you against a dead laptop, but not against yourself. If you delete or overwrite a file, the deletion syncs everywhere within seconds. Keep versioned backups (Time Machine, File History, Git) in addition to sync, and test that you can restore a file before the day you need to.

3.7 Site-Licensed Software
The University pays for a number of software licenses that you can use for free. The UO Software Downloads site at https://software.uoregon.edu (sign in with your Duck ID) offers MATLAB, Mathematica, LabVIEW, SPSS and SPSS Amos, ESRI ArcGIS, and more; some titles need a license code or a connection to the UO network or VPN to activate, and availability can differ between students and employees, so check the site for the current list. For Adobe products, students get Adobe Express on personal devices, while the full Creative Cloud suite is available in campus computer labs. UO-managed computers (as opposed to your personal laptop) install approved software through the Software Center app.
It is worth noticing that none of the tools at the center of this course, the shell, R, Python, Quarto, LaTeX, Git, VS Code, and Positron, require a license at all. 3.8 Managing References with Zotero
You will read hundreds of papers before your qualifying exam, and a reference manager is the only sane way to keep track of them. Zotero (https://www.zotero.org) is free and open source. Its browser connector saves a paper’s citation, and usually the PDF, from a journal page or PubMed with one click; group libraries let you share a reading list with your lab or rotation group; and it inserts citations and bibliographies into Word and into Quarto documents (Insert → Citation in the visual editor). Citing from Quarto is covered in Chapter 5, and a well-kept Zotero library makes it painless. Start now, while the library is small.

text:
3.10 Research Computing: RACS and Talapas
Research Advanced Computing Services (RACS), at https://racs.uoregon.edu, runs the University’s research computing and supports UO researchers with computing of every kind. Their best-known service is the Talapas HPC cluster, with CPU, GPU, and large-memory nodes and more than 225 scientific software packages installed. Beyond the cluster, RACS provides large-scale research data storage (roughly $35 per terabyte per year) for data that does not fit in what Talapas includes; Globus for fast, reliable transfer of very large datasets, for example from a sequencing core or a collaborator; consulting on software installation, code optimization, data security, and hardware purchases; grant support for the computing and data-management sections of proposals; and help reaching resources beyond UO, including national supercomputers through NSF ACCESS and cloud consulting for AWS and Azure. Contact them at racs@uoregon.edu or through the RACS service desk. They are there to help; ask early.

A single standard node has roughly ten times the cores and thirty times the memory of a laptop, and Talapas has hundreds of nodes. Your storage there consists of a 250 GB home directory plus your lab’s project space, 2 TB by default (Section 16.5). When an analysis reports “out of memory,” or would take days on your laptop, it is a job for Talapas. As Chapter 6 explains, memory is usually the binding constraint in data analysis, and the large-memory nodes exist precisely for the assemblies, image stacks, and single-cell matrices that will not fit anywhere else.


Getting an account
Every Talapas user is sponsored by a UO principal investigator and belongs to at least one PIRG (Principal Investigator Research Group), which the PI is responsible for. Ask your PI, or your rotation PI, to add you, and request the account through the Talapas customer portal at https://hpcrcf.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/1/group/1/create/9. A PI who does not yet have a PIRG can request one from racs@uoregon.edu. Setup can take a few days, so ask early; for this course, class access will be arranged before the Talapas material in Chapter 16. The Talapas Knowledge Base is the authoritative documentation.


Open OnDemand: Talapas in your browser
You do not need to master SSH (Section 16.4.1) to start using Talapas. Open OnDemand at https://ondemand.talapas.uoregon.edu gives you the cluster through a web browser; log in with your Duck ID using Chrome or Firefox (a private window avoids login glitches). Because OnDemand apps run as jobs on compute nodes, they keep running even after you close your browser, so remember to end sessions you no longer need.
