title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
D Part 1 - Common file formats
This appendix is a field guide to the file formats you will meet most often as a bioengineer working with data, and to the public repositories where published datasets, sequences, genomes, and structures live. It is meant to be scanned in about 15 minutes and returned to whenever you open an unfamiliar file or need to find a published dataset.
A useful first question for any file: is it plain text or binary? Plain-text files can be inspected with head, less, and grep, versioned with Git, and read by any language decades from now. Binary files are smaller and faster but need specific software to open.
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
section: D.1 Plain-text tables: CSV and TSV
text:
D.1 Plain-text tables: CSV and TSV
The workhorse of scientific data exchange. Each line is a row; columns are separated by commas (CSV, .csv) or tab characters (TSV, .tsv or .txt).
sample_id,material,stiffness_kPa,temp_C
S01,PEG_hydrogel,12.4,37
S02,PEG_hydrogel,13.1,37
S03,alginate,8.7,37

The first line is usually a header with column names.
Follow tidy data conventions (Lecture 02): one variable per column, one observation per row, one value per cell.
TSV is safer when text fields might contain commas (e.g., gene descriptions).
Read in R with readr::read_csv() / read_tsv(); in Python with pandas.read_csv() (add sep="\t" for TSV).
Quick shell checks: head file.csv, wc -l file.csv (rows + header), cut -d, -f3 file.csv | sort | uniq -c (tabulate column 3).
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
section: D.2 Spreadsheets: Excel (.xlsx) and its caveats
text:
D.2 Spreadsheets: Excel (.xlsx) and its caveats
Excel is fine for viewing and data entry, but it is risky as the only copy of your data:

Automatic conversion: Excel silently converts some values. Gene symbols such as SEPT2, MARCH1, and DEC1 have been turned into dates (“2-Sep”, “1-Mar”), and long numeric IDs are converted to scientific notation, losing digits. A 2016 survey found these errors in roughly one-fifth of papers with supplementary Excel gene lists (Ziemann et al., Genome Biology, https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-016-1044-7); HGNC later renamed several genes partly because of this. Keeping raw data in plain text and doing all manipulation in code is one of the core recommendations of “good enough” scientific computing practice (Wilson et al., 2017).
Hidden structure: merged cells, colors used as data, multiple tables per sheet, and formulas make files hard to read programmatically.
Proprietary binary format: .xlsx is a zipped XML bundle, so Git cannot show meaningful diffs.







Tip



Keep a CSV copy. Treat raw data as read-only, store a plain-text CSV (one sheet = one CSV) alongside any .xlsx, and do analysis in code. If you must import into Excel, use Data → From Text/CSV and set gene-name or ID columns to Text. In R, readxl::read_excel() reads .xlsx directly without Excel.
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
D.3 Sequences: FASTA
Plain text for DNA, RNA, or protein sequences. Each record is a header line starting with > followed by one or more lines of sequence:
>NM_000546.6 Homo sapiens tumor protein p53 (TP53), mRNA
CTCAAAAGTCTAGAGCCACCGTCCAGGGAGCAGGTAGCTGCTGGGCTCCGGGGACACTTTGCGTTCGGGC
TGGGAGCGTGCTTTCCACGACGGTGACACGCTTCCCTGGATTGGCAGCCAGACTGCCTTCCGGGTCACTG
>sp|P04637|P53_HUMAN Cellular tumor antigen p53
MEEPQSDPSVEPPLSQETFSDLWKLLPENNVLSPLPSQAMDDLMLSPDDIEQWFTEDPGP

Extensions: .fa, .fasta, .fna (nucleotide), .faa (amino acid), often gzipped (.fa.gz).
Used for reference genomes, transcripts, primers, and protein sequences.
No quality scores (contrast with FASTQ).
Count records: grep -c '>' file.fasta. List headers: grep '>' file.fasta | head.
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
D.4 Raw sequencing reads: FASTQ
Plain text with a strict 4-line-per-read structure (Table D.1):
@SRR12345.1 NS500126:1:H7TG3BGXY:1:11101:18923:1057
NCATGCAGCGTACGGTAATTGGCAGGCATTAGCAGCATCC
+
#AAAAFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF



Table D.1: The four lines of a FASTQ record









Line
Content




1
Header: read ID plus instrument, run, lane, tile, and x/y position. Starts with @


2
The sequence (A/C/G/T/N)


3
A + separator (sometimes repeats the header)


4
Per-base quality scores, one ASCII character per base, same length as line 2












NoteKey concept - Phred quality scores



Each quality character encodes a Phred score \(Q = -10 \log_{10}(P)\), where \(P\) is the probability that the base call is wrong (Table D.2):



Table D.2: Phred quality scores and the base-call accuracy they encode





Phred Q
Error probability
Base-call accuracy




10
1 in 10
90%


20
1 in 100
99%


30
1 in 1,000
99.9%


40
1 in 10,000
99.99%






Modern Illumina data use Phred+33 encoding: the character’s ASCII code minus 33 gives Q. So ! (ASCII 33) is Q0, + (43) is Q10, 5 (53) is Q20, ? (63) is Q30, and I (73) is Q40. In the example above, the leading # (Q2) on the N base signals a very low-confidence call.



Paired-end runs produce two files per sample, typically ..._R1_001.fastq.gz and ..._R2_001.fastq.gz; the reads in each file are in the same order.
Because each read is exactly 4 lines, number of reads = lines / 4: echo $(( $(zcat reads.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 )).
Quality-control tools such as FastQC summarize quality scores across a whole file.
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
D.5 Compressed files (.gz) and streaming
Sequencing and other large text files are almost always stored gzip-compressed (.gz), often 3-5x smaller. You rarely need to decompress them to disk; instead stream them through a pipe:
zcat reads.fastq.gz | head -n 8          # first two reads
zcat reads.fastq.gz | wc -l              # total lines
zcat genome.fa.gz | grep -c '>'          # number of sequences
zless annotation.gtf.gz                  # page through interactively

gzip results.tsv                         # compress (creates results.tsv.gz, removes original)
gunzip results.tsv.gz                    # decompress
gzip -k results.tsv                      # -k keeps the original
On macOS, the built-in zcat expects .Z files; use gzcat file.gz or zcat < file.gz instead. Some genomics files use bgzip (block gzip), which is still readable with zcat but also allows indexed random access (e.g., with tabix or samtools). Other archive types you will see: .zip (unzip), .tar.gz/.tgz (tar -xzf file.tar.gz), and .bz2 (bzcat).
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
D.6 Alignments: SAM and BAM
When reads are aligned to a reference genome, the result is stored as SAM (Sequence Alignment/Map; tab-delimited text with a @ header section and one line per alignment) or its compressed binary equivalent BAM (.bam, with an index .bai). Use samtools (Danecek et al., 2021; Li et al., 2009) to work with them (its sibling bcftools does the same for VCF):
samtools view -H sample.bam | head       # header lines
samtools view sample.bam | head -n 3     # first 3 alignments as SAM text
samtools flagstat sample.bam             # summary: how many reads mapped
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
section: D.7 Genomic annotation and interval formats
text:
D.7 Genomic annotation and interval formats
All are tab-delimited text, one feature per line; chromosome names must match the reference genome you use.

GFF3 / GTF (.gff3, .gtf): nine columns describing genes, transcripts, exons, and CDS features, 1-based coordinates. Reference annotation sets such as GENCODE (Frankish et al., 2021) and Ensembl are distributed in this form.
chr17  HAVANA  gene  7661779  7687538  .  -  .  gene_id "ENSG00000141510"; gene_name "TP53";
BED (.bed): at minimum chromosome, start, end; used for regions, peaks, and targets. 0-based, half-open coordinates (start is counted from 0 and the end position is excluded).
chr17  7661778  7687538  TP53  0  -
VCF (.vcf, .vcf.gz): genetic variants (SNPs, indels) relative to a reference, with ## metadata lines, a #CHROM header, and optional per-sample genotype columns.
#CHROM  POS      ID         REF  ALT  QUAL  FILTER  INFO
chr17   7675088  rs28934578 C    T    60    PASS    DP=42
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
section: D.8 Hierarchical binary data: HDF5, .h5, and .h5ad
text:
D.8 Hierarchical binary data: HDF5, .h5, and .h5ad
HDF5 (Hierarchical Data Format 5; .h5, .hdf5) stores many large numerical arrays and their metadata inside a single binary file organized like a file system (groups and datasets). It supports compression and lets programs read just the slice they need without loading the whole file, so it is common for microscopy and imaging data, simulation output, instrument data, and large matrices. .h5ad is the HDF5-based file format for Python’s AnnData package, widely used for large annotated matrices (e.g., samples/cells by genes).

Inspect from the shell with h5ls -r file.h5 (from the HDF5 tools).
Read in Python with h5py (or anndata.read_h5ad() for .h5ad); in R with the Bioconductor rhdf5 package.
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
section: D.9 R objects: .rds and .RData vs plain text
text:
D.9 R objects: .rds and .RData vs plain text

saveRDS(obj, "file.rds") / readRDS("file.rds") saves and restores one R object exactly (including factor levels, attributes, and complex objects such as model fits).
save(a, b, file = "file.RData") / load("file.RData") stores several objects and restores them under their original names (which can silently overwrite objects in your session).

Both are convenient for work in progress and for passing results between steps of your own pipeline, but they are not good archival or sharing formats: they are readable only by R, can break across major package versions, and cannot be diffed in Git. For anything you will share, publish, or keep long-term, also write a plain-text version (readr::write_csv()) and keep the code that regenerates the R object. Avoid saving your whole workspace to .RData at exit (set “Save workspace” to Never). See Chapter 11 and Appendix E.
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
section: D.10 Structured text: JSON and YAML
text:
D.10 Structured text: JSON and YAML
Both represent nested key-value data in plain text and are common for configuration files, metadata, pipeline parameters, and web APIs.
JSON (.json) uses braces, brackets, and quoted keys:
{
  "experiment": "hydrogel_swelling",
  "temperature_C": 37,
  "replicates": [1, 2, 3],
  "instrument": {"name": "rheometer", "geometry": "parallel plate"}
}
YAML (.yml, .yaml) expresses the same structure with indentation, and is what Quarto uses for document headers and _quarto.yml project files (Chapter 5):
experiment: hydrogel_swelling
temperature_C: 37
replicates: [1, 2, 3]
instrument:
  name: rheometer
  geometry: parallel plate
YAML is whitespace-sensitive: use spaces (never tabs) and keep indentation consistent. Read JSON with jsonlite in R or the json module in Python; jq is a handy command-line JSON tool. Many pipelines write a params.json or config.yaml describing a run; archive it with your outputs as the “lab notebook entry” for your computational analysis.

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
section: E.1 NCBI (US National Center for Biotechnology Information)
text:
E.1 NCBI (US National Center for Biotechnology Information)

GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus): processed functional-genomics data (expression tables, count matrices, sample metadata) from microarray and sequencing studies (Barrett et al., 2013). Series have GSE###### accessions, and each sample has a GSM###### record. When a paper says “data are available at GEO under GSE#####”, open the series page, check the sample list, and scroll to Supplementary file to download. In R, the Bioconductor GEOquery package (getGEO(), getGEOSuppFiles()) retrieves these directly.
SRA (Sequence Read Archive) (Leinonen et al., 2011): raw sequencing reads (FASTQ/BAM). Accessions: SRR (run), SRX (experiment), SRP (study). Use it when you need to re-process data from scratch. Files are big (often several to tens of GB per sample), so plan storage (e.g., Talapas project or scratch space, Lecture 08) before downloading.
GenBank / RefSeq: GenBank is the archive of all submitted nucleotide sequences; RefSeq is NCBI’s curated, non-redundant set of reference sequences (accessions like NM_ for mRNA, NP_ for protein, NC_ for chromosomes). Download records as FASTA from the page’s Send to menu or with NCBI’s datasets command-line tool.
BioProject / BioSample: the umbrella records that tie a study (PRJNA…) and its biological samples (SAMN…) to the associated GEO, SRA, and GenBank entries.







Tip



Getting raw reads. Two practical routes:

sra-tools on the command line: prefetch SRR12345678 then fasterq-dump --split-files SRR12345678 (gives paired _1.fastq and _2.fastq). On Talapas, look for it with module spider sra-tools, or install it with conda/Bioconda.
SRA Explorer: paste in an accession and it returns ready-to-use wget/curl download commands, usually pointing at the ENA mirror.
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
E.2 EBI / ENA (Europe)
The European Bioinformatics Institute runs the European counterparts: the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) mirrors SRA and GenBank (the same SRR… accessions work) and often provides direct FTP/HTTPS links to FASTQ files that you can wget without sra-tools. BioStudies / ArrayExpress is the European counterpart to GEO, and UniProt is the central resource for protein sequences and functional annotation.
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
section: E.3 Reference genomes and annotations: UCSC and Ensembl
text:
E.3 Reference genomes and annotations: UCSC and Ensembl

UCSC Genome Browser: interactive browser for genomes and annotation tracks, plus bulk downloads of genome FASTA, annotation files, and the Table Browser for exporting regions as BED/GTF. Assemblies are named like hg38 (human) or mm39 (mouse).
Ensembl: genome browser and annotation database with stable gene IDs (ENSG…) and a public FTP site for genome FASTA and GTF/GFF3 files for hundreds of vertebrate species (plus Ensembl Genomes for plants, fungi, bacteria, and invertebrates).

Always record which assembly and annotation release you used (e.g., GRCh38, Ensembl release number), because coordinates and gene models change between versions. Note also that UCSC names chromosomes chr1 while Ensembl uses 1.
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
section: E.4 Protein structures: Protein Data Bank
text:
E.4 Protein structures: Protein Data Bank
The RCSB Protein Data Bank (PDB) archives experimentally determined 3D structures of proteins, nucleic acids, and complexes, each with a four-character ID (e.g., 1TUP). Download coordinates as .pdb or the newer .cif (mmCIF) text formats; view them in the browser, or in tools like PyMOL or ChimeraX. The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database provides predicted structures for most known proteins.
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
section: E.5 General-purpose repositories: Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad
text:
E.5 General-purpose repositories: Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad
For data that do not fit a specialized repository (imaging, mechanical testing, simulation output, code, and supplementary tables), general-purpose repositories assign each deposit a permanent DOI so it can be cited:

Zenodo (run by CERN): free; integrates with GitHub to archive a tagged release of a code repository with a DOI.
Figshare: used by many journals for supplementary data.
Dryad: curated repository for data underlying publications, common in ecology, evolution, and biology.
crumbs: C  Common Data Formats & Public Repositories

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
E.6 How to choose
Table E.1 matches common needs to the repository that serves them.

title: Appendix C — Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
section: E.7 FAIR Data and Public Repositories
text:
E.7 FAIR Data and Public Repositories
Everything above is about finding and reading other people’s data. Sooner or later you will be on the other side: a journal, a funder (the NIH Data Management and Sharing Policy applies to all NIH-funded work since 2023), or a collaborator will ask for yours. Done well, sharing produces citations (reanalysis papers cite their input datasets), a one-line answer to “can I see your raw data?”, and compliance that passes review. Done poorly, the dataset sits on a lab drive until it is unreadable. The cost of doing it well is paid up front, during the project; the payoff lasts the lifetime of the data.

The FAIR Principles
Wilkinson et al. (Wilkinson et al., 2016) proposed four principles for data that people and machines can reuse (Table E.2).



Table E.2: The four FAIR principles (Wilkinson et al., 2016) and their practical consequences










Principle
One-line definition
What it means for you




Findable
Data and metadata have a persistent identifier and are indexed in a searchable registry
Get an accession (GEO, SRA, BioProject) or a DOI (Zenodo, Dryad); a lab website is not enough


Accessible
Anyone (or anyone authorized) can retrieve the data by that identifier through an open, standard protocol
HTTPS/FTP download; controlled access is fine for sensitive human data, as long as the procedure is open


Interoperable
Data use shared formats and controlled vocabularies so datasets combine cleanly
CSV/FASTA/FASTQ rather than proprietary formats; standard units; ontology terms rather than free text


Reusable
Provenance, a clear license, and enough metadata for someone else to reanalyze
README, data dictionary, software versions, license file






FAIR is not the same as open: patient genomes in a controlled-access archive can satisfy all four criteria. The principle most datasets fail is I: “B cells” in a free-text column is a different string from “B-cell”, “Bcell”, and “B_cell” to a computer, so every downstream integration needs a human to reconcile terms. The most common omission is F: data deposited without a stable identifier, or not indexed where searchers look.


Where Data Go: The NCBI Hierarchy
For sequencing-based studies the canonical archive is NCBI (mirrored by EBI/ENA), and its records nest (Table E.3). The same structure applies to bulk RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, genome resequencing, microbiome amplicons, and any other sequencing assay.



Table E.3: The NCBI record hierarchy for sequencing data











Record
Accession
What it holds
How many




BioProject
PRJNA######
The study as a whole: title, abstract, grant, publication
One per paper


BioSample
SAMN########
One biological sample: organism, tissue, donor or strain, treatment, collection date
One per sample


SRA run
SRR#######
The raw reads (FASTQ or BAM) from one sequencing run, linked to its BioSample (Leinonen et al., 2011)
One or more per sample


GEO series / sample
GSE###### / GSM######
Processed expression data: count matrices, normalized tables, and the sample metadata; GEO creates the SRA and BioSample records for you when you submit expression data (Barrett et al., 2013)
One series per study, one GSM per sample






The submission order follows the hierarchy: create the BioProject, register BioSamples, upload raw reads to SRA (each run linked to its SAMN), then, for expression studies, submit processed data and metadata to GEO, which links back to the BioProject and SRA runs. Cite every accession in the paper’s Data Availability statement. Non-sequencing data (imaging, mechanical testing, simulations, code) go to a general-purpose repository with a DOI (Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad, above).


The Canonical Sample Sheet
Most of the work of sharing is metadata, and the discipline that makes it painless is a single canonical sample sheet, started at experimental design time and kept under version control alongside your code. “Sample 1, Sample 2, Sample 3” is not metadata; at minimum the sheet answers who or what the sample came from, what tissue or material, what condition or treatment, what protocol, who processed it, when, on what instrument, with what software version. Its rules:

One row per sample, one column per variable (this is Chapter 8 applied to your experiment).
A stable, unique sample_id that never changes and appears in every file name, every FASTQ header you can control, and every downstream table. NCBI links BioSample, SRA, and GEO records by this ID, and the match is case-sensitive and literal: donor1_CTRL and Donor1_CTRL will not link. Manual retyping of sample names across three submission spreadsheets is the single most common cause of broken submissions.
Controlled vocabularies, not free text, for anything you will filter or join on: fixed spellings for conditions (control/treated, not ctrl, Control, CTRL), standard units in the column name (stiffness_kPa), ISO dates (2026-03-14), and, where an ontology exists, its term ID (Uberon for tissues, NCBI Taxonomy for organisms, Cell Ontology for cell types, EFO for assays; look them up at the Ontology Lookup Service).
Metadata columns for every batch effect you can record: extraction date, library prep kit and lot, sequencing run, operator. You cannot correct for a batch you did not write down.

sample_id      donor_id  tissue_ontology  condition  replicate  extraction_date  library_kit     run_id
donor1_ctrl    D001      UBERON:0000178   control    1          2026-02-03       TruSeq_v2_lot7  RUN_0412
donor1_treat   D001      UBERON:0000178   treated    1          2026-02-03       TruSeq_v2_lot7  RUN_0412
donor2_ctrl    D002      UBERON:0000178   control    2          2026-02-10       TruSeq_v2_lot7  RUN_0413
At submission time every upload template (BioSample, SRA, GEO) is derived programmatically from this one sheet with a few lines of dplyr::transmute() or pandas, so that names, dates, and IDs appear in exactly one place and inconsistencies are fixed there and propagate everywhere.


Plan Sharing at Design Time
The biggest mistake is thinking about deposition only when the manuscript is in revision. By then the sample metadata is scattered across several lab notebooks, the ontology terms have to be reconstructed from memory, and the person who ran the samples has graduated. Instead, at design time:

Start the canonical sample sheet with every column deposition will need, and update it as samples arrive.
Decide which repositories the data will go to and check their required metadata fields now, not later.
Keep raw data read-only in a clearly named directory (Section 16.5) and never edit it in place.
Record software versions and parameters for every processing step in the analysis code or a config.yaml (above).



Checksums, README, Data Dictionary, License
Four small files travel with a well-shared dataset.
Checksums prove that a file arrived intact. Compute one when you create or download a file and compare it after every transfer (repositories publish theirs; SRA and ENA list MD5 sums per file):
md5sum sample_R1.fastq.gz                    # prints a 32-character fingerprint
md5sum *.fastq.gz > checksums.md5             # record fingerprints for a directory
md5sum -c checksums.md5                       # later, or on another machine: verify
On macOS use md5 file or shasum -a 256 file. A single changed byte, a truncated download, or a job killed mid-write (see Section 16.9) produces a different checksum, which is far easier to notice than a subtly corrupt file.
A README (plain text or Markdown, at the top of the dataset) says what the data are, who generated them, when, with what instrument and protocol, how the files are organized, and how to cite them. A data dictionary describes every column of every table: name, meaning, type, units, allowed values, and how missing values are coded. Together they are what turns a directory of files into something a stranger can use.
A license states what others may do with the data; without one, reuse is legally ambiguous even if the files are public. Common choices are CC0 (public domain, the default at many repositories and the simplest for data) and CC BY (reuse with attribution); code is usually released under a software license such as MIT or GPL instead. Human-subject data may need a data-use agreement rather than an open license; your IRB and repository will say which.






Tip



A minimal FAIR checklist for any dataset. A persistent identifier (accession or DOI); open, plain-text formats where possible; a canonical sample sheet with stable IDs and controlled vocabularies; a README and data dictionary; recorded software versions; checksums; and a license. See also the GO FAIR initiative.

sed Patterns
# Basic substitution

# Using extended regex

# Capture groups

title: Appendix E — R Command Reference
text:
E.14 Common Gotchas






WarningThings that bite everyone




1-indexing. R counts from 1, and x[-1] drops the first element (it does not mean “the last” as in Python).
= vs ==. = assigns or names an argument; == tests equality. Using = where you meant == is a silent logic bug.
NA propagates. mean(c(1, NA, 3)) is NA; add na.rm = TRUE to ignore missing values.
Strings vs. factors. Older data.frame() code coerced text to factors; tibbles and R 4.0+ do not. If a character column behaves oddly, check its class().
Floating-point equality. 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is FALSE; compare with all.equal() or dplyr::near(), never ==, on decimals.
& vs &&. Use &/| on vectors (element-wise filtering) and &&/|| on single values inside if().
Recycling. Operating on vectors of different lengths silently recycles the shorter one; a warning appears only if the lengths are not multiples. Check length() when results look wrong.
Stale sessions. A package you just installed, or an object you deleted, may still be “there” in the running session. Restart R (Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + F10) before assuming something is broken (Section 2.13).

title: Appendix F — Python Quick Reference
text:
F.11 Common Gotchas






WarningThings that bite R users




0-indexing and half-open slices. x[0] is the first element, x[-1] is the last, and x[1:3] gives elements 1 and 2 only.
Indentation is syntax. Mixed tabs and spaces, or a missing colon before an indented block, produce IndentationError or SyntaxError. Use four spaces.
^ is not power. Use **; 2 ^ 3 is 1 (bitwise XOR).
Lists are not vectors. [1, 2] * 2 is [1, 2, 1, 2]; use NumPy arrays for element-wise math.
Mutability. y = x for a list or DataFrame makes y another name for the same object; changing one changes both. Use x.copy().
Population vs. sample SD. np.std(x) divides by n; use ddof=1 (or pandas .std()) to match R’s sd().
and/or vs &/|. Words for scalars; symbols (with parentheses) for arrays and DataFrame masks.
NaN != NaN. Test missing values with np.isnan() or pd.isna(), never == np.nan.
Which Python? If import pandas fails in the IDE but works in the terminal, the IDE is using a different interpreter or environment; check the interpreter picker.

title: Appendix G — SLURM Command Reference
text:
G.9 Job Arrays

Template: One Script, Many Samples
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=align
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --account=myPIRG
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --array=1-24%8               # 24 tasks, at most 8 running at once
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%A_%a.out   # %A = array job ID, %a = task ID
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x_%A_%a.err

set -euo pipefail
module purge
module load bwa/0.7.17 samtools/1.17

SAMPLE=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" samples.txt)   # line N = task N
OUT="results/${SAMPLE}.bam"
[[ -s "$OUT" ]] && { echo "$SAMPLE done, skipping"; exit 0; }   # resumable

bwa mem -t "$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK" ref.fa "raw/${SAMPLE}_R1.fastq.gz" "raw/${SAMPLE}_R2.fastq.gz" \
    | samtools sort -@ "$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK" -o "$OUT.tmp"
mv "$OUT.tmp" "$OUT"          # rename only after success: no truncated outputs
echo "Wrote $OUT"
Run mkdir -p logs results before submitting. The logs/ directory must exist or the job fails silently.


Array Index Variants
#SBATCH --array=0-100:10        # 0, 10, 20, ..., 100
#SBATCH --array=1-1000%50       # Max 50 running at once
#SBATCH --array=3,7,12          # Rerun only specific tasks
To size the array from a file at submit time: sbatch --array=1-$(wc -l < samples.txt) align.sh. To run a step only after every task succeeds: sbatch --dependency=afterok:ARRAY_JOB_ID next_step.sh.
